implementation_notes: try-with-resources declares the resource in the try header and the compiler emits close() on every exit path; if both the body and close() throw, the body's exception propagates and the close exception is attached through Throwable.getSuppressed instead of masking it. What replaces the classic wrapper is this statement plus the AutoCloseable contract: it covers exactly the resource-with-a-single-close protocol, accepts several resources (closed in reverse order of declaration), and since Java 9 an effectively final variable can be passed in without redeclaring it. Use the lambda wrapper below when the protocol is more than one close() - commit/rollback, retry, metrics - or when the resource is not AutoCloseable.
pitfalls: The resource must be declared in the try header (or be effectively final and named there, Java 9+); one created just before the try is not managed and leaks on the failure path.

close() should be idempotent and should not declare exceptions that must not be suppressed - the JDK advises keeping InterruptedException out of close() for exactly that reason, since suppressing it hides an interrupt.
A suppressed exception attached to the body's exception is easy to miss in logs; teardown failures that matter need to be surfaced by the caller.

variants.name: generic loan-pattern method taking a lambda body
variants.idiom_name: static <T> T withX(Supplier<T> / Function<Session, T> body)
variants.implementation_notes: For a protocol that is more than a single close(), pass the body as a lambda: the method opens the session, applies the function, commits, and rolls back when the lambda throws. Functional interfaces (Function, Consumer, Supplier, BiFunction) replace the anonymous inner classes that made this pattern painful before Java 8, and a dedicated @FunctionalInterface is the way to let the body throw checked exceptions. The wrapper is also the only way to hide a resource that does not implement AutoCloseable. Keep it for transactions, retries and audit or metric brackets; prefer try-with-resources for plain resources so the JDK's suppression rules apply.
pitfalls: Function.apply cannot throw checked exceptions, so a body that must throw needs its own @FunctionalInterface; wrapping checked exceptions in RuntimeException changes the API's failure contract.
A lambda capturing a loop variable sees the value it had at capture time (effectively final), not the loop's later mutations - pass the current value explicitly.
Boxing: Supplier<T> and Function<T, R> allocate for primitive results unless the primitive specializations (IntSupplier, ToIntFunction, ...) are used.
